I'm a literate adult with the capacity to understand something if I need to learn about it.

Is bitcoin something that the average Joe needs to know about, or is it something so esoteric that I'll never understand it? Will it enhance my life? Will I get rich from it? I live in the Middle east BTW so there's nothing out here yet.
I don't understand Bitcoins. Can anybody here help me understand whether I should spend anytime knowing about this.

If you dislike monetary inflation (the fact that most governments print money at will which devalues your savings intentionally), if you fear stiff monetary controls, if you hate bank fees such as overdraft, bounced check, maintenance or even just the time and hassle required to move your own money, then you should look to obtain some sort of significant value of Bitcoin.

If these items do not concern you, then Bitcoin probably isn't of any interest to you (yet).
Bitcoin uses a torrent-like public ledger thereby assuring you of the individual sender's credibility. Unlike a bank, you can't just add a bunch of zeros to the transactions and call it a loan.

Do you need to understand Bitcoin? That's actually an interesting question, in my opinion. I'm willing to bet (and I could be wrong) that you don't really know how credit cards and checks work. It sounds silly, we use them all the time, but very few people actually understand all the verification, clearing houses, cryptographic hashing, reconciliation and other esoteric stuff that goes on to make all of that work seamlessly for you. I think you can safely not understand Bitcoin the same way and just trust that it's doing its thing.

Can you trust Bitcoin? If you trust that a computer can scramble information in such a way that another computer can't unscramble it without a "key", then yes you can. Strong encryption has been around for a long time and hasn't been broken yet (unless backdoors are put in to make it easier to break) that we can be fairly sure that it won't be broken anytime soon. And Bitcoin has a very low chance of having a backdoor installed since all of it's code is open source and is being looked at by a lot of people who would spot something like that. So, yes, I think you can trust Bitcoin.

Will it enhance your life? Possibly. Since it's not controlled by a government and is bought and sold between people to set its price, it can't be inflated at a crazy rate and won't ever be in debt to another party like most currencies are today. This, of course, means that you don't want to trust a government to handle how much your money and savings are worth, which may or may not be true. If you do trust your government to make the best decisions for you, Bitcoin won't be all that exciting. If you don't, Bitcoin is a way to decouple yourself from another source of control the government and banks have over your life. This is why the people of Greece, Cyprus and Argentina are so interested in it. When there are government currency controls and bank lockdowns, Bitcoin starts to look a lot more interesting. You can't lock down Bitcoin. You can't limit withdrawals of Bitcoin. There's no central Bitcoin server or clearinghouse. Bitcoin is completely distributed and isn't even in a single country to be shutdown by that country's government. There's no real way to control it and that makes it especially valuable to people in countries that have very harmful currency policies.

Will you get rich from it? Probably not. You're just as likely to get poor from it as rich from it at this point, I think. As stated above, it really is a way to weaken the power of a government, so these governments could at anytime decide that they don't like it anymore and ban it. If you're someone who doesn't like conflict, you'll probably give up at this point and lose everything you had in Bitcoin, so you probably shouldn't get too much into it to begin with.

As a computer programmer, I'm really interested in Bitcoin since it's programmable money. To program with US dollars, I have to go through a third party to interact with the giant banking system that takes a cut, who goes through another third party that takes a cut, etc, etc. With Bitcoin, I can transact directly with the Bitcoin network and save on all those fees and do so with no interaction from me. It's an exciting new world that will be used more and more. Will it affect you? In some way it will, but I'm not sure if you'll need to spend the time to understand every little thing about it like I have.

It's like storing cash under your mattress instead of using banks and credit cards, except this cash is digital.

It's not hard to use but it comes with it's own set of hazards and currently, it's only useful for illegal activity and those who think the economy is about to collapse and everyone would run from the dollar to bitcoin, thus making early adopters rich.

That's a really good question!

Understanding how Bitcoin works coupled with a basic grasp of Theoretical Economics (aka 'Austrian' economics, or economics as the interactions of individual - often irrational - human action,) is enough to convince a thoughtful person that Bitcoin - or something very much like it - is the future of money. You don't need to understand these concepts to benefit though. You just need to know how to use it, which is not nearly as difficult as it first appears. If you can scan a QR code and enter a password you can use bitcoin. You have the option to have total control, and responsibility, for your own money. If you're comfortable trusting a large financial firm similar to a bank to protect your funds (afraid you might forget your password and lose it all) you have that option too.

The primary advantage to buying things with bitcoin is that it requires zero transfer of personal information. It's literally cold, hard digital cash. No name, credit or bank #'s, billing address etc. The primary advantage to selling for bitcoin is zero transaction fees and no charge-back losses. Once the cash is yours, it's yours. A private individual, with slight effort, can keep their finances entirely private. A public organization, can use the blockchain to transparently prove they are on the up-and-up, no complicated accounting analysis required.

Having just a bit of bitcoin today (pun) probably will either make you rich someday (at the very least you'll have some liquid, spendable currency when bank money is carried in wheelbarrows for a loaf of bread,) or it will be worthless. Pretty much one or the other at this point. Don't put all your eggs in one basket, but definitely use caution with the bank basket that's ready to unravel.

On a side note, imagining a world economy lubricated by an intrinsically deflationary currency; to trust that your cash savings will have the same or greater purchasing power when you retire - without the need to earn interest - is an exciting potential from the perspective of sharia finance law.
